title: RH Lean proof: verification files
content_html:
Verification files for the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis

Announced at alpo.ge/remark.pdf on 20 November 2026.

Andrew Sutherland (MIT), checks run with Claude Code. Page last updated 2026-11-22 14:10 UTC. Results below are as of that time and this page will be updated as the remaining checks finish.

Summary

The published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, two independently written kernels, nanoda and con-leche, accept the full exported proof, and lean4lean accepts every compiled module. The --compare modes of con-leche and of its Rust port con-ron, independent implementations of Comparator's statement matching, each confirm all five theorems against the challenge. An independent sandboxed lake build of the archive reproduces the export byte for byte. The lake comparator run and the Lean-kernel replay of the export are still in progress.

What was verified

Five theorems, proved in the submission's Main.lean. Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (riemannZeta, DirichletCharacter, DirichletCharacter.LFunction, IsPrimitive) are Mathlib's.

1. The Riemann Hypothesis, using Mathlib's own definition (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition s ≠ 1 is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

def RiemannHypothesis : Prop :=
  ∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis

2. The same statement written out in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function. For every modulus N ≥ 1 and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at s = 1, where the L-function has its pole.

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

5. The same for primitive characters, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

Scope. "GRH" here means Dirichlet L-functions: all moduli and all characters. Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions and automorphic L-functions in general are not among the statements that were checked.

Arithmetic consequences

As a check that does not depend on Mathlib's definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with kimihiro64/Robin1984 (commit acab1a3), an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria on the same Lean and Mathlib versions. Importing both gives two theorems about the divisor sum, with no hypotheses and no mention of zeta (ArithSolution.lean; statements alone in ArithChallenge.lean, which imports only Mathlib):

theorem robin_inequality :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 5040 < n →
      ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) <
        Real.exp Real.eulerMascheroniConstant * (n : ℝ) * Real.log (Real.log (n : ℝ))

theorem lagarias_inequality :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
      ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤
        (harmonic n : ℝ) + Real.exp (harmonic n : ℝ) * Real.log (harmonic n : ℝ)

The elaborated statement of the Lagarias inequality

The kernels check elaborated terms, not source text, so what was verified is the term that Lean's elaborator produces from the statement. For the Lagarias inequality that term is short enough to read in full. This is the statement printed with set_option pp.all true, so that every coercion, instance, implicit argument and universe level is shown, as elaborated against Mathlib alone (Lean v4.33.1, Mathlib 0df444a3), with none of the proof loaded:

def lagariasStmt : Prop :=
∀ (n : Nat),
  @LT.lt.{0} Nat instLTNat (@OfNat.ofNat.{0} Nat (nat_lit 0) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 0))) n →
    @LE.le.{0} Real Real.instLE
      (@Nat.cast.{0} Real Real.instNatCast
        (@DFunLike.coe.{1, 1, 1} (@ArithmeticFunction.{0} Nat (@MulZeroClass.toZero.{0} Nat Nat.instMulZeroClass)) Nat
          (fun (x : Nat) => Nat)
          (@ArithmeticFunction.instFunLikeNat.{0} Nat (@MulZeroClass.toZero.{0} Nat Nat.instMulZeroClass))
          (ArithmeticFunction.sigma (@OfNat.ofNat.{0} Nat (nat_lit 1) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 1)))) n))
      (@HAdd.hAdd.{0, 0, 0} Real Real Real (@instHAdd.{0} Real Real.instAdd)
        (@Rat.cast.{0} Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n))
        (@HMul.hMul.{0, 0, 0} Real Real Real (@instHMul.{0} Real Real.instMul)
          (Real.exp (@Rat.cast.{0} Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n)))
          (Real.log (@Rat.cast.{0} Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n)))))

It names 27 constants directly: Nat, Real, the order and arithmetic instances on them, the casts from Nat and Rat to Real, ArithmeticFunction.sigma, harmonic, Real.exp and Real.log. Its meaning depends on 1,801 Mathlib and core declarations in all, counting definitions with their bodies and theorems by their statements only (a proof cannot change what a definition means). The corresponding count for Robin's inequality is 2,050; the difference is mostly the definition of Euler's constant.

Files: the script, its output (both statements), and the dependency lists for Lagarias and Robin.

Check it yourself

With Lean v4.36.0 installed, nothing needs to be built. You need roughly 100 GB of RAM and 70 GB of disk.

zstd -d --long=30 solution.ndjson.zst      # --long=30 is required
zstd -d --long=27 challenge.ndjson.zst
sha256sum solution.ndjson challenge.ndjson  # compare with the hashes above

lake comparator --config comparator.json \
  --challenge-from-export challenge.ndjson --solution-from-export solution.ndjson

nanoda alone took about 28 minutes on 80 threads. The Lean kernels are single-threaded and take much longer.

The fastest independent check is con-leche built from source (Lean v4.36.0, about two minutes to build). It needs about 50 GB of RAM and took under four minutes on 64 threads:

git clone https://github.com/leanprover/con-leche && cd con-leche
git checkout compare        # 5dc36dc1; master (cd2eceab) for the plain check
lake build con-leche
.lake/build/bin/con-leche --compare challenge.ndjson solution.ndjson

Caveats

  • How the original build was done, and the rebuild that checks it. The original build ran on cloud machines without a sandbox, and compiled each file by calling lean directly with the same inputs lake supplies (module name, package name and the lakefile's options), not through lake build. All the kernel checks above were run on the export from that build. We then repeated the build on a separate machine with lake build Main inside a bubblewrap sandbox: no network, the source tree read-only, only .lake writable, the archive downloaded afresh from the author's site, and Mathlib's files checked against the official cache first. The export made inside that sandbox is byte-identical to the published one, so every check on the published export applies to it.
  • The per-file .olean hashes depend on the build directory, and one module is not deterministic. In Lean v4.33.1 a compiled file stores each linter message together with the absolute path of its source file. Of our 175,187 compiled files, 98,219 contain the path /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean/src/…; the other 76,968, including Main.olean, contain no path. So project-oleans.sha256 can be reproduced only by a build whose source tree is at /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean; elsewhere, only the files of modules that emit no linter messages should match.
    The sandboxed lake build was run at that same path, and 175,186 of its 175,187 files are byte-identical to our manifest. The exception is Formalism/LocalToGlobal/SiegelLatticeTheory/CokernelGLCounts/RankPointCounts/LocModel.olean: same size, different contents. Recompiling that one module six times on one machine with identical inputs gave one output four times and the other twice, and those are exactly the two hashes in the two manifests. The two outputs differ in 38 bytes: the name of one bound variable in BBtop.eq_1, an equation lemma that Lean generates automatically the first time a proof asks for it. Two adjacent theorems in the file both ask for it, Lean elaborates theorem bodies in parallel, and the lemma takes that variable's name from whichever theorem gets there first. Bound-variable names play no part in kernel checking, so the two files are logically the same. The export is not affected, and the export from the sandboxed build is byte-identical to ours: an export contains only the declarations that the five theorems depend on, and BBtop.eq_1 is not one of them, because the proofs that caused it to be generated do not refer to it. We checked that this name does not occur in the export. Had a proof on the dependency path referred to such a lemma by name, two builds could have produced exports with different hashes, although every check would still have passed on either. Compiled single-threaded (lean -j1), the module gave the same output six times out of six. A ten-line file with no imports reproduces the behaviour: on Lean v4.33.1 and v4.34.1 it compiles to two different outputs with -j32 and to one with -j1; on v4.36.0 it gave one output in 40 runs. The same race, with the first caller's options in place of its names, was reported as Lean issue #15498 and fixed by pull request #15499, first released in v4.36.0. That change also removes this behaviour: the file gives two outputs on the nightly builds of 7 and 8 October 2026 and one output in 40 runs on those of 9 and 10 October and on the toolchain built from the pull request alone. Because of this module, the sha256 of the whole manifest file is not reproducible even at the same path; compare file by file.
  • A passing check shows that the formal statements, as written in Lean against Mathlib's definitions, follow from the three standard axioms according to the kernels used. It relies on those kernels and on Mathlib's definitions being what they are intended to be.

All the kernel checks above were run on the export from that build. We then repeated the build on a separate machine with lake build Main inside a bubblewrap sandbox: no network, the source tree read-only, only .lake writable, the archive downloaded afresh from the author's site, and Mathlib's files checked against the official cache first. The export made inside that sandbox is byte-identical to the published one, so every check on the published export applies to it. The per-file .olean hashes depend on the build directory, and one module is not deterministic. In Lean v4.33.1 a compiled file stores each linter message together with the absolute path of its source file. Of our 175,187 compiled files, 98,219 contain the path /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean/src/…; the other 76,968, including Main.olean, contain no path. So project-oleans.sha256 can be reproduced only by a build whose source tree is at /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean; elsewhere, only the files of modules that emit no linter messages should match. The sandboxed lake build was run at that same path, and 175,186 of its 175,187 files are byte-identical to our manifest. Recompiling that one module six times on one machine with identical inputs gave one output four times and the other twice, and those are exactly the two hashes in the two manifests. The two outputs differ in 38 bytes: the name of one bound variable in BBtop.eq_1, an equation lemma that Lean generates automatically the first time a proof asks for it. Two adjacent theorems in the file both ask for it, Lean elaborates theorem bodies in parallel, and the lemma takes that variable's name from whichever theorem gets there first. Bound-variable names play no part in kernel checking, so the two files are logically the same. The export is not affected, and the export from the sandboxed build is byte-identical to ours: an export contains only the declarations that the five theorems depend on, and BBtop.eq_1 is not one of them, because the proofs that caused it to be generated do not refer to it. We checked that this name does not occur in the export. Had a proof on the dependency path referred to such a lemma by name, two builds could have produced exports with different hashes, although every check would still have passed on either. Compiled single-threaded (lean -j1), the module gave the same output six times out of six. A ten-line file with no imports reproduces the behaviour: on Lean v4.33.1 and v4.34.1 it compiles to two different outputs with -j32 and to one with -j1; on v4.36.0 it gave one output in 40 runs. The same race, with the first caller's options in place of its names, was reported as Lean issue #15498 and fixed by pull request #15499, first released in v4.36.0. That change also removes this behaviour: the file gives two outputs on the nightly builds of 7 and 8 October 2026 and one output in 40 runs on those of 9 and 10 October and on the toolchain built from the pull request alone. Because of this module, the sha256 of the whole manifest file is not reproducible even at the same path; compare file by file. A passing check shows that the formal statements, as written in Lean against Mathlib's definitions, follow from the three standard axioms according to the kernels used. It relies on those kernels and on Mathlib's definitions being what they are intended to be.

• The per-file .olean hashes depend on the build directory, and one module is not deterministic. In Lean v4.33.1 a compiled file stores each linter message together with the absolute path of its source file. Of our 175,187 compiled files, 98,219 contain the path /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean/src/…; the other 76,968, including Main.olean, contain no path. So project-oleans.sha256 can be reproduced only by a build whose source tree is at /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean; elsewhere, only the files of modules that emit no linter messages should match.
    The sandboxed lake build was run at that same path, and 175,186 of its 175,187 files are byte-identical to our manifest. The exception is Formalism/LocalToGlobal/SiegelLatticeTheory/CokernelGLCounts/RankPointCounts/LocModel.olean: same size, different contents. Recompiling that one module six times on one machine with identical inputs gave one output four times and the other twice, and those are exactly the two hashes in the two manifests. The two outputs differ in 38 bytes: the name of one bound variable in BBtop.eq_1, an equation lemma that Lean generates automatically the first time a proof asks for it. Two adjacent theorems in the file both ask for it, Lean elaborates theorem bodies in parallel, and the lemma takes that variable's name from whichever theorem gets there first. Bound-variable names play no part in kernel checking, so the two files are logically the same. The export is not affected, and the export from the sandboxed build is byte-identical to ours: an export contains only the declarations that the five theorems depend on, and BBtop.eq_1 is not one of them, because the proofs that caused it to be generated do not refer to it. We checked that this name does not occur in the export. Had a proof on the dependency path referred to such a lemma by name, two builds could have produced exports with different hashes, although every check would still have passed on either. Compiled single-threaded (lean -j1), the module gave the same output six times out of six. A ten-line file with no imports reproduces the behaviour: on Lean v4.33.1 and v4.34.1 it compiles to two different outputs with -j32 and to one with -j1; on v4.36.0 it gave one output in 40 runs. The same race, with the first caller's options in place of its names, was reported as Lean issue #15498 and fixed by pull request #15499, first released in v4.36.0. That change also removes this behaviour: the file gives two outputs on the nightly builds of 7 and 8 October 2026 and one output in 40 runs on those of 9 and 10 October and on the toolchain built from the pull request alone. Because of this module, the sha256 of the whole manifest file is not reproducible even at the same path; compare file by file.

Verification files for the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis

Announced at alpo.ge/remark.pdf on 20 November 2026.

Andrew Sutherland (MIT), checks run with Claude Code. Page last updated 2026-11-22 14:10 UTC. Results below are as of that time and this page will be updated as the remaining checks finish.

概括

The published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, two independently written kernels, nanoda and con-leche, accept the full exported proof, and lean4lean accepts every compiled module. The --compare modes of con-leche and of its Rust port con-ron, independent implementations of Comparator's statement matching, each confirm all five theorems against the challenge. An independent sandboxed lake build of the archive reproduces the export byte for byte. The lake comparator run and the Lean-kernel replay of the export are still in progress.

What was verified

Five theorems, proved in the submission's Main.lean. Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (riemannZeta, DirichletCharacter, DirichletCharacter.LFunction, IsPrimitive) are Mathlib's.

1. The Riemann Hypothesis, using Mathlib's own definition (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition s ≠ 1 is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

def RiemannHypothesis : Prop :=
  ∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis

2. The same statement written out in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function. For every modulus N ≥ 1 and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at s = 1, where the L-function has its pole.

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

5. The same for primitive characters, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

范围。 "GRH" here means Dirichlet L-functions: all moduli and all characters. Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions and automorphic L-functions in general are not among the statements that were checked.

Arithmetic consequences

As a check that does not depend on Mathlib's definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with kimihiro64/Robin1984 (commit acab1a3), an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria on the same Lean and Mathlib versions. Importing both gives two theorems about the divisor sum, with no hypotheses and no mention of zeta (ArithSolution.lean; statements alone in ArithChallenge.lean, which imports only Mathlib):

theorem robin_inequality :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 5040 < n →
      ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) <
        Real.exp Real.eulerMascheroniConstant * (n : ℝ) * Real.log (Real.log (n : ℝ))

theorem lagarias_inequality :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
      ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤
        (harmonic n : ℝ) + Real.exp (harmonic n : ℝ) * Real.log (harmonic n : ℝ)

The elaborated statement of the Lagarias inequality

The kernels check elaborated terms, not source text, so what was verified is the term that Lean's elaborator produces from the statement. For the Lagarias inequality that term is short enough to read in full. This is the statement printed with set_option pp.all true, so that every coercion, instance, implicit argument and universe level is shown, as elaborated against Mathlib alone (Lean v4.33.1, Mathlib 0df444a3), with none of the proof loaded:

def lagariasStmt : Prop :=
∀ (n : Nat),
  @LT.lt.{0} Nat instLTNat (@OfNat.ofNat.{0} Nat (nat_lit 0) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 0))) n →
    @LE.le.{0} Real Real.instLE
      (@Nat.cast.{0} Real Real.instNatCast
        (@DFunLike.coe.{1, 1, 1} (@ArithmeticFunction.{0} Nat (@MulZeroClass.toZero.{0} Nat Nat.instMulZeroClass)) Nat
          (fun (x : Nat) => Nat)
          (@ArithmeticFunction.instFunLikeNat.{0} Nat (@MulZeroClass.toZero.{0} Nat Nat.instMulZeroClass))
          (ArithmeticFunction.sigma (@OfNat.ofNat.{0} Nat (nat_lit 1) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 1)))) n))
      (@HAdd.hAdd.{0, 0, 0} Real Real Real (@instHAdd.{0} Real Real.instAdd)
        (@Rat.cast.{0} Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n))
        (@HMul.hMul.{0, 0, 0} Real Real Real (@instHMul.{0} Real Real.instMul)
          (Real.exp (@Rat.cast.{0} Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n)))
          (Real.log (@Rat.cast.{0} Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n)))))

It names 27 constants directly: Nat, Real, the order and arithmetic instances on them, the casts from Nat and Rat to Real, ArithmeticFunction.sigma, harmonic, Real.exp and Real.log. Its meaning depends on 1,801 Mathlib and core declarations in all, counting definitions with their bodies and theorems by their statements only (a proof cannot change what a definition means). The corresponding count for Robin's inequality is 2,050; the difference is mostly the definition of Euler's constant.

The sandboxed lake build was run at that same path, and 175,186 of its 175,187 files are byte-identical to our manifest. The exception is Formalism/LocalToGlobal/SiegelLatticeTheory/CokernelGLCounts/RankPointCounts/LocModel.olean: same size, different contents. Recompiling that one module six times on one machine with identical inputs gave one output four times and the other twice, and those are exactly the two hashes in the two manifests. The two outputs differ in 38 bytes: the name of one bound variable in BBtop.eq_1, an equation lemma that Lean generates automatically the first time a proof asks for it. Two adjacent theorems in the file both ask for it, Lean elaborates theorem bodies in parallel, and the lemma takes that variable's name from whichever theorem gets there first. Bound-variable names play no part in kernel checking, so the two files are logically the same. The export is not affected, and the export from the sandboxed build is byte-identical to ours: an export contains only the declarations that the five theorems depend on, and BBtop.eq_1 is not one of them, because the proofs that caused it to be generated do not refer to it. We checked that this name does not occur in the export. Had a proof on the dependency path referred to such a lemma by name, two builds could have produced exports with different hashes, although every check would still have passed on either. Compiled single-threaded (lean -j1), the module gave the same output six times out of six. A ten-line file with no imports reproduces the behaviour: on Lean v4.33.1 and v4.34.1 it compiles to two different outputs with -j32 and to one with -j1; on v4.36.0 it gave one output in 40 runs. The same race, with the first caller's options in place of its names, was reported as Lean issue #15498 and fixed by pull request #15499, first released in v4.36.0. That change also removes this behaviour: the file gives two outputs on the nightly builds of 7 and 8 October 2026 and one output in 40 runs on those of 9 and 10 October and on the toolchain built from the pull request alone.
